chapters.relation: Foreword by Elio M. Garcia and Linda Antonsson (founders of Westeros.org). They argue that Martin's epic succeeds because its real subject is 'the human heart in conflict with itself': unlike Tolkien-style epics with a Dark Lord and morally obvious heroes, A Game of Thrones gives characters in shades of gray - Ned wrestling with honor and honesty, Jon with vows versus love, Tyrion craving his father's approval - and presents this volume's essays as illumination of that moral complexity, from Littmann's Hobbes-as-maester to Jacoby on warg consciousness.

chapters.file: ch07 - Game of Thrones and Philosophy.md
ch08 - Game of Thrones and Philosophy.md
ch09 - Game of Thrones and Philosophy.md
chapters.relation: Henry Jacoby's introduction frames the volume around mortality: winter is coming, all men must die (valar morghulis), yet through honor, duty, and philosophy 'first we'll live' meaningful lives. Playing on Arya's mantra 'fear cuts deeper than swords,' he claims logic cuts deeper still - swords defend bodies, but logic defends our ideas, beliefs, and values - leaning on Socrates' claim that no evil can befall a good person, since the virtuous soul stands in harmony against desire and influence. He previews the essays: Hobbes as a maester, the dark side of chivalry, Robb's questionable war, Arya and Zen, and Ned's need of Machiavelli.

chapters.file: ch10 - Game of Thrones and Philosophy.md
ch11 - Game of Thrones and Philosophy.md
chapters.relation: Greg Littmann asks who should rule Westeros and answers with Hobbes's Leviathan: people act only from self-interest ('we are all Lord Littlefinger under the skin') and fight for gain, safety, and glory - the mountain clans, Robert's preemptive strike on Daenerys, Drogo's wars for pride - so without a sovereign life is a war of all against all, and only an absolute ruler makes oath-keeping self-interested. Mapping Hobbes's own civil war (the Stuarts onto the Targaryens), he argues that even Varys is right to serve 'the realm' and peace by betraying Ned, and that loyalty rightly transfers from Aerys to Robert to Joffrey because protection, not lineage or justice, is the point of the sovereign. He then criticizes Hobbes: Ned and Jon show people really do die for principle, and Mad King Aerys's overcentralized power left rebellion as the only remedy - the War of the Five Kings shows civil war's horror must be weighed against appeals to honor.

chapters.file: ch12 - Game of Thrones and Philosophy.md
chapters.relation: Don Fallis starts from Joffrey's lie about Arya and the butcher boy Mycah - which costs Mycah's life and Sansa's direwolf Lady's - to dissect lying versus other deception in Westeros: Catelyn accusing Tyrion is not lying because she believes it, Ned's coerced confession at the Great Sept is a real lie (Austin's duress excuse fails, as Thomas More's counterexample shows), and Ned's silence about Joffrey's parentage before the dying Robert is deception by withholding that he himself mistakes for lying. He asks whether lying is morally worse than misleading - Kant and Chisholm say yes, Williams and Scanlon no - testing breach of invited trust (Mirri Maz Duur's 'only death may pay for life'), responsibility-shifting to the audience ('That was a lie you told yourself'), and preserved autonomy (Kant's Groundwork, Mill's On Liberty). Finally, is it worse to lie to a king? Consequentialism explains the danger of misleading the powerful, oaths of fealty and divine right suggest a special duty, but Locke's demolition of divine right (seconded by Monty Python) leaves only the punishment, not the wrongdoing, greater.

chapters.file: ch13 - Game of Thrones and Philosophy.md
chapters.relation: Marcus Schulzke reads the War of the Five Kings through The Prince: who wins the Iron Throne is decided by virtu - skill adapted to shifting circumstances - against fortuna, and morality is no guide, since actions are good or bad only as they gain or hold power. The failures illustrate the lessons: Viserys's arrogance binds him to the wrong allies, Robert's emotions make him capricious, Joffrey makes himself hated instead of feared, Ned's uncompromising honesty and trust in Littlefinger destroy him, and Robb's dependency on Walder Frey's auxiliary forces proves fatal. The true Machiavellians are the mask-wearers - Littlefinger, Arya, Jon as lion-and-fox - and above all Tyrion, who wins the Blackwater by planning, and Daenerys, who builds her own army from freed slaves and so makes her own luck.

chapters.file: ch14 - Game of Thrones and Philosophy.md
chapters.relation: Richard H. Corrigan tests Robb Stark's war against Joffrey with just war theory, criteria for resorting to war (legitimate authority, just cause, right intention, last resort, probability of success, proportionality) and for conduct (discrimination, treatment of prisoners, no reprisals). Robb is a legitimate authority acclaimed King in the North, offers rejected peace terms, and fights cleanly - Jaime is humanely held at Riverrun while Sansa is beaten by Joffrey, and Gregor Clegane's murders, rapes, and the Dothraki sack of the Lhazareen mark the other side's atrocities. Yet Corrigan concludes Robb fails right intention: his dominant motive is vengeance for his father, not the free North he professes, so although we root for him, his war cannot strictly be called just.

chapters.file: ch15 - Game of Thrones and Philosophy.md
ch16 - Game of Thrones and Philosophy.md
chapters.relation: Eric Silverman argues Game of Thrones explodes the storybook link between virtue and worldly happiness: Ned, 'one man in ten thousand,' is betrayed and executed, so Plato's claim that the just person is happy must mean psychic order rather than material flourishing - reason ruling spirit and appetite - as with Bran, who flourishes as a greenseer though he will never walk again. Cersei is Plato's tyrant, her soul ruled by insatiable appetite and paranoia, so no external goods can ever satisfy her, while Aristotle's correction - virtue necessary but not sufficient for eudaimonia, which also needs health, friends, and good fortune - explains why both Ned (virtue without external goods) and Cersei (goods without virtue) end up unhappy. Finally he inverts Pascal's Wager: since playing the game of thrones risks total loss (torture, humiliation, death) for limited gain, and even winning hollows you out - Robert confesses he was 'never so alive as when I was winning this throne or so dead as now that I've won it' - only a fool would play.

chapters.file: ch17 - Game of Thrones and Philosophy.md
chapters.relation: David Hahn contends Ned died because of his honor, not for it. Hobbes explains why: words bind no one without fear of enforcement - Cersei ripping up Robert's will ('Is this meant to be your shield, Lord Stark?') exposes Ned's belief that allegiance alone secures the King's Justice - and the Iron Throne itself is a Leviathan, forged by Aegon's dragons ending the state of nature, whose force rather than justice holds the peace. Machiavelli supplies the indictment of Ned's idealism: 'we who presume to rule must do vile things for the good of the realm,' so Ned's refusal to assassinate Daenerys, his merciful warning to Cersei, and backing the rightful but war-prone Stannis over Renly cost him his head and plunged the realm into civil war; the security of the state demanded exiling or killing the Lannisters and crowning Renly.

chapters.file: ch18 - Game of Thrones and Philosophy.md
chapters.relation: Albert Anglberger and Alexander Hieke contrast Ned, the virtue ethicist's genuinely good man, with Cersei, a 'minimally extended' egoistic consequentialist whose only morally relevant subjects are herself and her children. Aristotle's apparatus does the work: phronesis lets Ned rank his daughters' lives above honesty when he confesses falsely ('the lies we tell for love'), his 'you're too fat for your armor' quip shows the golden mean among competing virtues, and Cersei's unbalanced maternal love is excess, hence not a virtue. They then unsettle moral judgment itself: utilitarianism would license the Slaver's Bay slaveholders, virtue ethics lacks action rules and cross-cultural agreement (charity is no Dothraki virtue), and Martin's POV narration gives direct access to Ned's inner life but only Varys's and Littlefinger's unreliable reports about Cersei - so our verdicts on her, like real-life judgments of others, rest on shaky evidence.

chapters.file: ch19 - Game of Thrones and Philosophy.md
chapters.relation: Matthew Tedesco reads Bran's coma and Drogo's living death as biomedical ethics: Jaime's 'good clean death' for Bran raises active versus passive euthanasia, and with James Rachels he argues the AMA's killing/letting-die distinction merely licenses more suffering, while Brock recasts withdrawal of treatment as intentional killing anyway. The Bran case frames end-of-life decisions for children - the Johns Hopkins and Baby John Pearson cases - and whether parents may weigh a handicap's burden on the family, a question made vivid by Bran riding Hodor. Dany's smothering of Drogo, by contrast, does not strike readers as murder because personhood rather than biological humanity carries moral standing: on Tooley's self-consciousness, Warren's five criteria, or Marquis's future-like-ours, Drogo is human but no longer a person - which leads straight to Peter Singer's claim that killing a disabled infant who is not a person may not be wrong at all, leaving us to ask whether our recoil is reason or taboo.

chapters.file: ch20 - Game of Thrones and Philosophy.md
ch21 - Game of Thrones and Philosophy.md
chapters.relation: Henry Jacoby wields Westeros's strange beings against the mind-body problem: Nagel's 'what it is like' question becomes 'What is it like to be a direwolf?', and wargs like Bran-in-Summer and Orell's eagle ask whether one point of view can literally inhabit another. Against Descartes's denial of animal consciousness (only language users have souls; Mormont's raven crying 'Corn!' is a machine), he argues Ghost's pain behavior and direwolf physiology ground animal consciousness exactly as our brothers' behavior grounds theirs. Wargs do not refute materialism - in Westeros magic violates physical law without invoking nonphysical stuff - and 'Zombie Sansa', the philosophers' phenomenal zombie, together with the reanimated wights, is impossible in our world (with Russell, experiences are brain events known directly) and conceivable beyond the Wall only because the supernatural breaks the laws of nature.

chapters.file: ch22 - Game of Thrones and Philosophy.md
chapters.relation: Edward Cox asks whether physicalism - everything is physical, and everything depends on the arrangement of physical stuff - is true in Westeros. The causal argument shows Jaime's love could move Bran's body only if it is itself a brain state, and the maesters' science (boiling wine against infection, Baratheon black hair as heredity, the Eyrie's winch) reveals a world running on our physics. But magic strains the picture: reanimated Othor and Jafer Flowers must physically change to walk, and Daenerys's walk into Drogo's pyre requires her resolve to disrupt combustion itself - so Cox concludes magic is either violation of physical law or a nonphysical force, and that in our world immaterial souls would be exactly as improbable as magic.

chapters.file: ch23 - Game of Thrones and Philosophy.md
chapters.relation: Abraham Schwab turns Ygritte's 'You know nothing, Jon Snow' into a theory of epistemic humility: Jon misreads wildling courtship norms, Sam's dragonglass shatters on wight Small Paul, Lord Mormont assumes Mance fights like a southern king and pays for it at the Fist of First Men, while Arya's accurate self-knowledge keeps her alive. Formalizing with justified true belief - Sam's lucky dagger thrust is not knowledge, and the Watch's warranted belief that the dead Othor was harmless justifies falsity - he uses Lysa's letter, which sent Ned to King's Landing on a lie, to ask what justification is: Descartes's absolute certainty is too strict, reliabilism vindicates testimony ('dark wings, dark words'), so that only Sansa need witness Ned's beheading for the Starks to know it, and between Melisandre's circular dogma about Azor Ahai and total skepticism, moderate skepticism best governs belief - a humility the south lacked about the Horn of Winter.

holes.name: Lying vs Other Deception
holes.what: The distinction between asserting something you believe false (lying) and misleading without asserting it, plus the debate over whether lying is morally worse than other deception.
holes.why: Chapter 12's entire argument - Joffrey's lie, Ned's coerced confession, Cersei's unspoken incest, Mirri Maz Duur's implication - turns on this distinction, which the taxonomy lacks.

holes.name: Personhood (person vs human being)
holes.what: The bioethics distinction between being biologically human and being a person with full moral standing, cashed out via consciousness, rationality, and self-awareness.
holes.why: Chapter 19 defends Daenerys's killing of Drogo on the ground that he is human but no longer a person (Tooley, Warren, Marquis, Singer), a concept the taxonomy lacks apart from Frankfurt's specific second-order-desires account.

holes.name: Physicalism
holes.what: The metaphysical thesis that everything that exists is physical and every feature of the world depends on the arrangement of physical stuff.
holes.why: Chapter 22 defines and defends physicalism, then uses Westeros's magic (wights, Daenerys's fire immunity) to ask whether souls could exist only by violating physical law.
